Where it began

Dawid Malan was born in Roehampton, in London, on 3 September 1987. When he was seven his family moved to South Africa, and he went to school at Paarl Boys' High. It was a sporting household. His father played for Western Province B, his brother Charl played first-class cricket for Loughborough MCCU, and his sister Liné played field hockey for South Africa.

He began with Boland, then came back to England and joined Middlesex in July 2006, playing a Twenty20 match against Surrey on the day he arrived. He stayed more than a decade, made 132 not out on his first-class debut in 2008 and later captained the county in all three formats.

The player

England gave him his Test debut against South Africa in July 2017. That winter, at the WACA in Perth, he made his first Test hundred, the first by an England batter in that Ashes series. In 22 Tests from 2017 to 2022 he scored 1,074 runs at 27.54, with one hundred and nine fifties, and in 2021 he returned against India and made 70.

The shortest format was where he shone brightest. He made 78 and was man of the match on his Twenty20 international debut in 2017, hit a 48-ball hundred in New Zealand in 2019 and in September 2020 rose to first place in the world rankings for the format. A few months later his rating reached 915, then the highest ever recorded.

What made him special

Once he settled in he was thrilling to watch. He became, at the time, the fastest batter to 1,000 runs in Twenty20 internationals, needing only 24 innings, and in 2022 he made 125 against the Netherlands as England piled up a record 498 in a one-day international. That made him the first England man with a hundred and a wicket in every format.

The wicket part took some patience. His leg-breaks were an occasional extra, and his two Test wickets cost 65.50 each, but every bowler knows the price is soon forgotten and the wicket never is.

Away from the middle

He was part of the England squad that won the 2022 T20 World Cup and retired from international cricket in August 2024. He moved from Middlesex to Yorkshire in 2020, and that summer made his first double hundred, 219 in the Bob Willis Trophy. He has played Twenty20 leagues around the world, winning the Pakistan Super League with Peshawar Zalmi, and in November 2025 he signed to play Twenty20 for Gloucestershire. He supports Liverpool.

And finally

England picked him for his first one-day international in 2019, nearly two years after his Test debut, when several World Cup players were being rested. He took the chance in his own good time: when he retired, only four men had a higher one-day batting average.
